overview: The male golden whistler is one of the brightest birds of the eastern forests: golden-yellow below with a black head, a white throat framed by a black band and a yellow collar. Females are soft grey-brown. Both have a strong, musical song, best known as a run of whistled notes that ends in a loud, whip-like crack.

deep_dive.habitat: Almost any wooded habitat from rainforest and tall wet forest to dry woodland and mallee, mostly in the denser parts; sometimes parks and orchards.
deep_dive.range: Eastern and southern Australia, from Queensland down the east coast through Victoria and Tasmania and across the south to Western Australia (the western birds are sometimes split off as a separate species). Most birds stay put, though some in the south-east move north or to lower ground in winter. South-eastern mainland birds belong to subspecies youngi, Tasmanian ones to glaucura.
deep_dive.behaviour: Usually forages alone in the lower and middle levels of trees, gleaning insects, spiders and other small invertebrates from leaves and bark, plus some berries, and sometimes joins mixed-species flocks. Breeds September to January; both sexes build a shallow bowl nest bound with spider web, share the incubation of 2-3 eggs for about 15 days and feed the young.
deep_dive.voice: A strong, musical and varied voice. The best-known song is a series of repeated whistled notes that builds to a loud whip-like ending ('wi-wi-wi-wi-whit'), and there is also a rising 'seep' call. Females sing too. In our recordings the whistled notes sit at about 2-3.6 kHz (median about 3-3.4 kHz), the final whip-crack is a very fast upward or downward sweep covering roughly 2-7 kHz, and upslurred calls reach about 7-8 kHz.
deep_dive.anatomy: A songbird (order Passeriformes). Like all songbirds it has a tracheobronchial syrinx: the voice box sits where the windpipe splits into the two bronchi, so there is a sound source on each side that can be controlled separately. About 16-18 cm long and 25 g, with a rather big, rounded head (the genus name Pachycephala means 'thick head'). The bill is short, stout and black in males (dark brown in females) and the eyes are red-brown. (No whistler-specific syrinx study was consulted; these points are general songbird anatomy.)
